topics.title: 22.1 Virtual addresses
topics.summary: A virtual address is interpreted in an address-space context. The same numeric address in two processes can designate unrelated objects. The meaning of an address also changes over time when a mapping is removed and another mapping occupies the same range. Do not infer usable address-space size from pointer size alone. A 64-bit pointer representation does not imply that all 64 bits are available as independent implemented virtual-address bits. x86-64 configurations support particular address widths and canonical-address rules. The examples here use explicitly stated simplified widths rather than treating one hardware configuration as universal.

topics.title: 22.2 Physical addresses
topics.summary: A physical address identifies a location in the processor’s physical address map. That map can include ordinary memory and regions associated with devices; physical does not mean that every possible address corresponds to an installed DRAM byte. The operating system manages physical frames and establishes mappings that connect them to virtual pages. Applications normally neither choose arbitrary frames nor rely on a mapping remaining attached to one frame forever. Moving or replacing backing storage is possible as long as the required observable behavior is preserved and the translation machinery is updated correctly.

topics.title: 22.3 Address translation
topics.summary: Translation maps a virtual address to a physical address while checking the requested access. A useful teaching decomposition is virtual address = virtual page number + page offset . The page number selects a mapping; the offset identifies the byte within that page. With equal-sized pages and frames, translation preserves the offset. Translation is therefore not an arbitrary byte-by-byte lookup. Contiguous bytes within one mapped page share the same mapping and permissions at the paging granularity. An access that spans a page boundary can involve more than one translation and can encounter different permissions on the two pages.

topics.title: 22.4 Memory isolation
topics.summary: Separate address-space mappings allow the kernel to keep one process’s private storage inaccessible to another. Permission checks further distinguish reads, writes, instruction fetches, and user versus supervisor access, subject to the architecture and configuration. The word private requires context. A private mapping can initially share physical storage through copy-on-write while preserving logically private modification semantics. Isolation describes what each process is allowed to observe and change, not necessarily whether every byte has a unique physical copy at every instant.

topics.title: 22.5 Shared memory
topics.summary: Shared memory deliberately maps common storage into more than one execution environment. A store through one mapping can become visible through another according to the platform’s memory and synchronization rules. This avoids copying every message through a separate transfer buffer, but it does not remove the need for a communication protocol. Shared-memory programs must define ownership, synchronization, initialization, and recovery from participant failure. They must also avoid assuming equal virtual base addresses. An offset of 128 bytes from the shared region’s base is portable across mappings of that region; an ordinary process-local pointer stored there may not be.

topics.summary: Assume 4-KiB pages. Process A maps virtual page 4 to physical frame 12; process B maps virtual page 4 to physical frame 27. Both load from virtual address 0x4123 . The virtual page number is 0x4 , and the offset is 0x123 . A reaches physical address 0xC123 ; B reaches 0x1B123 . The same pointer bits do not imply shared data. Now suppose A maps virtual page 8 and B maps virtual page 9 to physical frame 30. A’s 0x8080 and B’s 0x9080 both identify physical address 0x1E080 . These calculations illustrate two independent properties: equal virtual addresses can refer to different storage, and different virtual addresses can refer to shared storage. They say nothing by themselves about access permission or synchronization. A correct access requires the mapping and the requested operation to be allowed.

SLIDE 1: Chapter 22 — Virtual Address Spaces

LECTURE NARRATION
A pointer used by an ordinary process usually identifies a location in that process’s virtual address space. It is not a direct index into installed DRAM. Translation lets the system place data in physical storage independently of the addresses used by the program, share selected storage, and reject accesses that violate mapping permissions. Virtual memory is not simply “using disk as extra RAM.” Paging to storage is one possible policy built on translation. Isolation, controlled sharing, sparse address spaces, and flexible placement are useful even when every actively used page remains in physical memory. [ R3 , R10 ]

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. SLIDE 12: 22.5 Shared memory

Shared memory deliberately maps common storage into more than one execution environment.
